Italian B1 · citizenship exam

Study Master

1,897 words in 72 semantic sections, plus 363 verbs in Part II — 2,260 unique entries in all. Sections 6 to 8 re-sort verbs you have already met, and a few words carry two parts of speech, so neither adds to that total.

Read one section at a time, not the whole list. Each section is a small field of meaning, so the words you already know act as hooks for the ones beside them.

Click any word to open an example sentence with its translation. The most common words (tiers 1 and 2) carry two examples. Click again to close; several can stay open at once.

Context on the row is a short warning only — a false friend, an unexpected gender. The full explanation, the examples and any related words are inside the drawer.

The Plural column is filled only when the plural is worth knowing: irregulars, words that switch gender, and words that never change.

Printing: Cmd+P → Save as PDF. Set to A4 landscape. Every example opens automatically on paper.

Part I — People and relationships

Family — core relations13 words

The nucleus: the people in your own household. — 13 words

Family — core relations
ItalianPluralEnglish
la famigliaf.le famigliefamily

Context

Family, in both the household sense and the wider sense of relatives. It turns up constantly on forms: stato di famiglia is the certificate listing everyone registered at your address, and ricongiungimento familiare is the family-reunification procedure. In casual speech, essere di famiglia means someone is treated as one of your own.

Examples

La mia famiglia vive ancora all'estero.

My family still lives abroad.

Passo il Natale con la famiglia.

I spend Christmas with my family.

il genitorem.i genitoriparent

Context

This is the word for a parent

Examples

I miei genitori vivono ancora in India.

My parents still live in India.

il padrem.i padrifather

Context

Masculine even though it ends in -e

Examples

Mio padre è arrivato in Italia nel duemila.

My father came to Italy in the year 2000.

Mio padre lavora ancora.

My father still works.

la madref.le madrimother

Context

Feminine even though it ends in -e

Examples

Mia madre vive ancora in India.

My mother still lives in India.

Mia madre cucina benissimo.

My mother cooks very well.

il papàm.invariable (m.)dad

Context

Informal, the way a child says it

Examples

My dad helped me with the move.

Context

Informal, the way a child says it

Examples

il figliom./f.i figlison, child

Context

Examples

la figlianoun, f.le figliedaughter
il fratellom.i fratellibrother

Context

Examples

Mio fratello ha due anni più di me.

la sorellaf.le sorellesister

Examples

Mia sorella si sposa a giugno.

il maritom.i maritihusband

Examples

My husband cooks on Saturdays.

la moglief.le mogliwife

Context

Irregular plural ending

Examples

familiareadj.family, familiar

Feminine

Same in the feminine — it ends in -e.

Examples

Greetings, politeness and social formulas24 words

Fixed expressions: openings, closings, thanks, wishes, yes and no. — 24 words

Greetings, politeness and social formulas
ItalianPluralEnglish
ciaointerj.hi, bye

Context

For friends, family and children only. Saying ciao to an official, a doctor or a shopkeeper you do not know reads as rude — use buongiorno or salve instead.

Examples

Ciao, come stai?

Hi, how are you?

Ciao ragazzi, a domani!

Bye everyone, see you tomorrow!

salveinterj.hello

Context

The safe middle ground: warmer than buongiorno, more respectful than ciao, and it works at any hour. When you cannot tell how formal to be, this is the one to reach for.

Examples

Salve, vorrei un'informazione.

Hello, I would like some information.

buongiornointerj.good morning, hello

Context

Safe greeting until mid-afternoon

Examples

Buongiorno, vorrei rinnovare il permesso.

Good morning, I would like to renew my permit.

buonaserainterj.good evening

Context

Good evening, and it starts earlier than English speakers expect — from mid-afternoon in much of Italy, roughly once the shops reopen. Using buongiorno at six in the evening sounds off.

Examples

Buonasera, ho un appuntamento alle sei.

Good evening, I have an appointment at six.

buonanotteinterj.good night

Examples

Buonanotte, a domani!

Good night, see you tomorrow!

arrivederciinterj.goodbye

Examples

Grazie di tutto, arrivederci!

Thank you for everything, goodbye!

addiointerj.farewell, goodbye

Examples

Addio, non ci vedremo più.

Farewell, we will not see each other again.

benvenutoadj.welcome

Feminine

Feminine: benvenuta.

Examples

Benvenuti in Italia!

Welcome to Italy!

pregointerj.you're welcome, please

Context

The most overworked word in Italian courtesy. It answers grazie as 'you're welcome', invites someone to go ahead or sit down, and asks someone to repeat themselves. Tone and context carry the meaning.

Examples

Prego, si accomodi.

Please, take a seat.

Prego, dopo di lei.

Please, after you.

grazieinterj.thank you

Examples

Grazie mille per il suo aiuto.

Thank you very much for your help.

Grazie di tutto.

Thank you for everything.

il favorem.i favorifavour

Context

Masculine even though it ends in -e

Examples

Mi può fare un favore?

Can you do me a favour?

Per favore, chiuda la porta.

Please close the door.

il signorem./f.i signorigentleman, sir

Context

Polite way to address an unknown man

Examples

Buongiorno signore, come posso aiutarla?

Good morning sir, how can I help you?

Il signore alla cassa è gentile.

The gentleman at the till is kind.

la signoranoun, f.le signorelady, madam
l'auguriom.gli auguriwish, greeting

Context

Said in the plural for birthdays and holidays

Examples

Tanti auguri di buon compleanno!

Best wishes for a happy birthday!

saluteinterj.bless you, cheers

Context

Health, and also what you say when someone sneezes. Alla salute! is a toast. Il Servizio Sanitario Nazionale is the public health system, which residents can register with.

Examples

Salute! Ti sei preso il raffreddore?

Bless you! Have you caught a cold?

Salute! Alla tua!

Cheers! To you!

cin cininterj.cheers

Examples

Cin cin, alla vostra salute!

Cheers, to your health!

coraggiointerj.come on, cheer up

Context

Said to cheer somebody up

Examples

Coraggio, manca poco!

Come on, it is nearly over!

Coraggio, ce la fai!

Come on, you can do it!

forzainterj.come on

Context

Shouted to encourage, especially at sport

Examples

Forza, ce la puoi fare!

Come on, you can do it!

Forza, manca poco!

Come on, not much left!

aiutointerj.help!

Examples

Aiuto! C'è stato un incidente!

Help! There has been an accident!

Aiuto! Non so nuotare!

Help! I cannot swim!

bastainterj.that's enough

Context

Enough; also 'that's all' when ordering

Examples

Basta così, grazie!

That's enough, thank you!

Basta, non voglio più parlarne.

Enough, I do not want to talk about it any more.

eccophrasehere is, there you are

Examples

Ecco i documenti che mi ha chiesto.

Here are the documents you asked me for.

Ecco il tuo caffè.

Here is your coffee.

okinterj.OK, all right

Examples

Ok, ci vediamo alle tre.

OK, see you at three.

Ok, va bene così.

OK, that is fine.

behinterj.well...

Examples

Beh, non lo so proprio.

Well, I really do not know.

Beh, vediamo cosa succede.

Well, let's see what happens.

ehinterj.eh, right

Examples

Fa freddo oggi, eh?

It is cold today, isn't it?

Che caldo, eh!

It is hot, isn't it!

il Comunem.i Comunimunicipality, town council

Context

The town hall and the smallest unit of Italian local government. Almost every civic errand starts here: registering your address, requesting certificates, booking the citizenship oath. Written with a capital C it means the institution; lower case, comune is the adjective 'common'.

Examples

Devo iscrivermi all'anagrafe del Comune.

I have to register with the council's registry office.

Il Comune rilascia il certificato.

The town hall issues the certificate.

l'anagrafef.le anagrafiregistry office, civil registry

Context

The registry office inside your Comune that holds births, deaths, residence and marriage records. This is where you register your address and collect the certificates almost every other application asks for.

Examples

Sono andato all'anagrafe per il certificato di residenza.

I went to the registry office for the residence certificate.

la questuraf.le questurepolice headquarters

Context

Police headquarters. This is where you handle residence permit applications and renewals, criminal record certificates and most immigration paperwork. Every province has one. Different from the Carabinieri, who are military police and handle serious crime, and from the Polizia Municipale, who deal with traffic and local matters. You will almost certainly go here during the citizenship process.

Examples

Devo andare in questura per le impronte.

I have to go to the police headquarters for fingerprints.

la prefetturaf.le prefettureprefecture

Context

The government's local office, headed by the prefetto. Citizenship applications are decided here, and the oath is usually sworn at the Comune afterwards.

Examples

Ho un appuntamento in prefettura giovedì.

I have an appointment at the prefecture on Thursday.

La prefettura risponde per lettera.

The prefecture replies by letter.

il prefettom.i prefettiprefect

Examples

Il prefetto ha firmato il documento.

The prefect signed the document.

l'ambasciataf.le ambasciateembassy

quindiconj.therefore, so

Context

Therefore, so. Draws a conclusion from what came before. Slightly more formal than allora and, unlike it, genuinely logical rather than merely conversational.

Examples

Mancava la firma, quindi l'hanno respinta.

Era chiuso, quindi sono tornato.

perciòconj.so, therefore

Examples

pertantoconj.therefore, hence

alloraadv.then, so

Context

A filler and a hinge: 'so', 'right then', 'well'. Opens sentences, buys thinking time, and signals that you are about to get to the point. Extremely common in speech and best avoided in formal writing.

Examples

Allora, cosa facciamo stasera?

infatticonj.in fact, indeed

cioèconj.that is, in other words

Rephrases what you just said

ossiaconj.that is, in other words

Examples

comunqueconj.anyway, however

Context

Very common filler: anyway, in any case

Examples

altrimentiadv.otherwise, or else

Examples

sennòconj.otherwise, or else

Examples

magariadv.maybe, if only

A very common word with no clean English equivalent. Depending on context it means 'maybe', 'if only!' or 'I wish'. Used constantly in speech. If someone asks Vieni alla festa? and you answer Magari!, you mean 'I'd love to but probably can't'. With a past subjunctive it expresses regret: magari fossi andato, 'if only I had gone'.

Part II — Verbs

Every verb in the deck lives here. The first five sections sort them by the pattern they follow, and between them each verb appears exactly once. The last three re-cut the same verbs — by auxiliary, by preposition, and by meaning — for when you want to revise a different way.

Open any verb for all seven tenses, every person in a sentence. A verb marked mastered stays marked wherever it turns up.

Section 6 — Verbs whose past tense uses essere99 verbs

With these the ending agrees with who is speaking. Grouped by why they take essere. — 99 verbs

Movement from A to B (14)

Where the verb takes you somewhere, or away from it.

andare, venire, arrivare, partire, tornare, ritornare, entrare, uscire, salire, scendere, cadere, correre, volare, emigrare

Change of state (19)

Becoming something you were not before.

nascere, morire, crescere, diventare, cambiare, aumentare, diminuire, migliorare, guarire, scadere, finire, cominciare, iniziare, riuscire, nevicare, piovere, esistere, risultare, succedere

Staying put (7)

The opposite of movement — still essere.

Reflexive verbs (49)

Every single one, without exception.

Section 7 — Verbs with an obligatory preposition54 verbs

The little word is not optional: leaving it out is the commonest B1 mistake. — 54 verbs

a + plain verb

The second verb keeps its dictionary form.

cominciare — to start doing
iniziare — to begin doing
continuare — to keep doing
imparare — to learn to do
insegnare — to teach someone to do
aiutare — to help someone do
riuscire — to manage to do
provare — to try to do
andare — to go and do
venire — to come and do
mettersi — to set about doing
invitare — to invite someone to do

di + plain verb

By far the commonest pattern after an opinion verb.

finire — to finish doing
smettere — to stop doing
cercare — to try to do
decidere — to decide to do
dimenticare — to forget to do
ricordarsi — to remember to do
sperare — to hope to do
pensare — to plan to do
credere — to believe you are doing
chiedere — to ask to do
dire — to tell someone to do
promettere — to promise to do
permettere — to allow someone to do
evitare — to avoid doing
consigliare — to advise someone to do
proporre — to suggest doing

a + person or thing

The object needs the little word a in front of it.

telefonare — to phone someone
rispondere — to answer someone
chiedere — to ask someone
dire — to say to someone
scrivere — to write to someone
mandare — to send to someone
dare — to give to someone
piacere — to be liked by someone
pensare — to think about something
credere — to believe in something
giocare — to play a sport or game
partecipare — to take part in
servire — to be useful for something
assistere — to attend an event

di + person or thing

Often where English uses about, of, or nothing at all.

parlare — to talk about something
occuparsi — to deal with something
trattare — to be about a subject
ricordarsi — to remember something
dimenticarsi — to forget something
innamorarsi — to fall in love with
preoccuparsi — to worry about something
interessarsi — to be interested in
accorgersi — to notice something
fidarsi — to trust someone
avere paura — to be afraid of
avere bisogno — to need
